covering.note: Its skin is grainy and greenish brown on top.

diet.note: Insects, crabs, fish, snails, small mammals and smaller frogs.

trees.note: Older frogs sometimes rest on rocks, but not up in branches.

young.note: A female lays several hundred eggs at a time.

clues.text: It is the biggest frog on Earth, up to 32 cm long.
Its eyes can be almost 2.5 cm across.
Its belly and the undersides of its legs are yellowish orange.
It needs big, clean, fast-flowing rivers deep in the rainforest.
It rests on wet, mossy rocks by rivers and waterfalls.
It has no vocal sac, so it can't croak. Males whistle with their mouths open instead.
To escape, it can skitter across the water in up to seven short leaps.
Main threat: hunting for food. Its numbers fell by more than 70% in 15 years.
Some were shipped to the USA for zoos, pets and even frog-jumping races.
Adults clear out pools by the river, or dig hollows in the gravel bank, to lay their eggs in, and guard the nests at night.

facts.text: A big one weighs about as much as a newborn baby.
Its tadpoles eat only one kind of water plant, which grows near waterfalls.
Building its nests means moving large, heavy objects, which may be why it grew so big.
For such a big frog, its mating call is high-pitched, and it can last up to a minute and a half.
Young goliath frogs spend most of their time underwater.
On land it tires after five or six leaps, which makes it easy for people to catch.
Its eggs stick to plants on the river bottom. Tadpoles grow for about 75 to 90 days.
New roads to plantations make its rivers easier for hunters to reach.
Hunters prefer the biggest frogs, usually females. Far from towns, goliath frogs are more common and grow bigger.
